names.name: Coptic cross tattoo
names.said: in Egyptian Arabic the mark is simply the salib, the cross
names.th: รอยสักกางเขนคอปติก

text.what: A small cross tattooed on the inside of the right wrist. The usual design is the Coptic cross: two bold lines of equal length crossing at right angles, each arm ending in three points — twelve points in all. Often blue. In a Cairo studio it takes under ten minutes.
text.story:
Many Copts have the cross tattooed as a sign of faith on the inside of their right arm at the wrist. That is the whole of what the Coptic cross article says about it, and every other thing on this page had to be sourced elsewhere, which is itself worth noticing about a practice this widespread.

The Egyptian Streets writer Farah Rafik, in February 2022, traces the tattooing tradition among Egyptians to the Coptic period, and says it intensified after the Muslim conquest of Egypt around 640 CE, when Christians faced conversion or the religious tax, and some were marked with crosses on the wrist so the authorities could tell who had kept their faith. What began as a mark applied from outside became a mark applied by parents. Rafik quotes the researcher Jean-Philippe Belleau: "The fear of conversion among members of the Christian minority of Egypt has led many Coptic parents to tattoo their children with a small blue cross." The reason parents gave was blunt — a child whose parents were killed would still be recognised, and raised, among Christians. In some churches the wrist has also served as the check at the door.

The people who put it on are named and working. Girgis Gabriel Girgis has run a studio in Muqattam, the quarter above Cairo, for over thirty years, and does five to seven tattoos a day, mostly Coptic crosses. Another tattooist, Magdy Girgis, calls the practice "a sign of resistance, perseverance and solidarity".

*Inference —* this is the only amulet in this batch whose bearer cannot take it off, sell it, lose it or leave it to anybody, and the tradition's own account of why it is permanent is exactly that.

The sign has Egyptian company. The ankh survived Christianisation in Egypt as the crux ansata, an ankh with a circular loop, and Coptic Christians used that form in many media, especially in textiles. Bertran de la Farge dates the trefoil Coptic cross to the fourth century and reads it as a predecessor of the Occitan cross.
text.how: Applied by a tattooist, usually on the inside of the right wrist, commonly in childhood within Coptic families and also on adults. The design is small and fast. The sources read here name no rite, no fasting and no blessing attached to it; what they describe is a studio, a queue and a needle.
text.today: Living, and worked at daily. As of 2026 Girgis Gabriel Girgis's Muqattam studio is the one the reporting names, and the mark functions as a permanent visible sign of Christian identity. Whether a reader outside the community should wear the same design is an argument with named people in it, and this atlas reports it rather than settling it: the tattooists quoted describe the mark as resistance and solidarity, which is a claim about who is inside.

dating.period: the Coptic period to the present
dating.label: from around the seventh century CE to now
dating.note: Rafik traces tattooing among Egyptians to the Coptic period and dates the intensification of the cross mark to after the Muslim conquest of Egypt, around 640 AD; 640 is that figure. The Coptic period begins earlier and the source does not date the practice's start within it, so the from_year is the first year the source attaches a number to, not the first year a Copt wore a cross.

object.inscription: none; the design is the Coptic cross — four equal arms, each ending in three points for the Trinity, twelve points in all for the Apostles, often with a circle at the centre
object.note: single_use is true in the sense that matters here: it cannot be transferred, removed or inherited.
